title: Quick Ratio: Acid-Test Liquidity
subtitle: Excludes inventory - stricter than the Current Ratio
openingQuestion: How does the Quick Ratio differ from the Current Ratio?
openingOptions: The Quick Ratio is used for small businesses
The Quick Ratio uses total assets
The Quick Ratio excludes inventory because it's hard to convert to cash quickly
explanation: The quick ratio also measures short-term solvency but strips inventory out of the numerator, because goods sitting in a warehouse can take months to sell and usually have to be discounted if sold urgently. The gap between the two ratios is the valuable piece of information: a large gap means a company's ability to pay depends heavily on selling its goods - which isn't guaranteed to happen exactly when the cash is most needed.

realWorldExample.description: Seasonal fashion chains often show a large gap between Current Ratio and Quick Ratio, because most of their current assets sit in seasonal clothing inventory - an asset type that can lose value quickly and be hard to sell out if the season is missed, making the Quick Ratio a far more accurate reflection of real liquidity.

quiz.question: Which industry needs to watch the Quick Ratio most closely?
options: Banks, because their assets are mostly loans
Fashion retail, where inventory easily goes out of season
Management consulting, because its main cost is salaries
Software, because revenue is recognized by period
quiz.explanation: Seasonal retail (fashion, electronics) carries large inventory that can become obsolete. Current Ratio might look good while Quick Ratio is low, better reflecting real liquidity risk.

quiz.question: Why is a large gap between a company's Current Ratio and Quick Ratio a warning signal worth paying attention to?
options: Because receivables grew faster than revenue during the period
Because the company is holding too much unproductive cash
Because liquidity is depending on selling off inventory
Because current liabilities are unusually larger than long-term debt
quiz.explanation: The Quick Ratio excludes inventory precisely because it's the least liquid and riskiest current asset - easily losing value (going out of style, out of season) and not certain to sell quickly at full price. A large gap between the two ratios warns that the company is depending too heavily on selling its inventory to ensure liquidity.

quiz.question: Current assets are 600 billion, of which inventory is 250 billion; current liabilities are 300 billion. What is the Quick Ratio?
options: 1.83 (= (600 − 50) ÷ 300, subtracting the wrong inventory figure)
2.0 (= 600 ÷ 300, forgetting to subtract inventory - that's the Current Ratio)
0.83 (= 250 ÷ 300, using only the inventory portion)
1.17 (= (600 − 250) ÷ 300, inventory correctly subtracted)
quiz.explanation: Quick Ratio = (Current Assets − Inventory) / Current Liabilities = 350/300 = 1.17. The Current Ratio is 2.0 - the gap between the two figures shows nearly half of current assets sit in unsold goods.

quiz.question: A fashion chain has a Current Ratio of 2.5 but a Quick Ratio of only 0.6. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: Its ability to pay short-term debt depends on selling off inventory
The company is safe because its Current Ratio is above 2.0
The company lacks enough goods to sell during peak season
The company's current liabilities have been under-recorded this period
quiz.explanation: A Quick Ratio of 0.6 means cash and receivables cover only 60% of current liabilities. The rest depends on selling off inventory - exactly the type of asset that can lose 50-70% of its value if a season is missed.

quiz.question: For a software company, the Current Ratio and Quick Ratio are nearly identical. Why?
options: Because software is recorded entirely as an intangible asset
Because it has almost no inventory to subtract
Because deferred revenue automatically makes the two ratios equal
Because accounting standards don't allow software companies to hold inventory
quiz.explanation: The two ratios only differ by the inventory portion. With no inventory, there's nothing to subtract, so for software and services, calculating the Quick Ratio adds almost no additional information.

keyTakeaways: The Quick Ratio excludes inventory from current assets
Stricter and more realistic than the Current Ratio
Especially important for industries with large, obsolescence-prone inventory

practicePrompt.question: A retailer has Current Assets = 500 billion (of which Inventory = 300 billion), Current Liabilities = 300 billion. Current Ratio = 500/300 ≈ 1.67 (looks fine). But what about the Quick Ratio, and why is it stricter?
options: The Quick Ratio exactly equals the Current Ratio since both formulas use the same current assets and current liabilities
Quick Ratio = (500-300)/300 ≈ 0.67, because inventory is stripped out of current assets
The Quick Ratio is always higher than the Current Ratio because it adds in the company's long-term investments
The Quick Ratio doesn't apply to retail since retail always carries a lot of inventory
practicePrompt.explanation: The Quick Ratio (Acid-Test Ratio) excludes inventory from current assets because it's the least liquid asset, needing time to sell and convert into cash. In this example, a Quick Ratio ≈ 0.67 (below 1) shows that if the company had to repay debt urgently without time to sell its inventory, it could face real liquidity difficulty - a stricter lens than the Current Ratio.

summary.keyIdea: The Quick Ratio excludes inventory from current assets
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Stricter and more realistic than the Current Ratio

application.title: Calculate the Quick Ratio
application.message: For the same company from the previous lesson, remove Inventory from Current Assets and recalculate the Quick Ratio - see how much or little the number shifts compared to the Current Ratio.
application.secondary: A large gap between these two ratios tells you how dependent the company is on inventory.

sections.text: The Quick Ratio is a stricter version of the Current Ratio: it excludes inventory from current assets, because inventory isn't always sellable quickly or at full cost.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: Quick Ratio = (Cash + Marketable Securities + Accounts Receivable) / Current Liabilities
Why inventory has to be excluded

Among the three main types of current assets - cash, receivables, and inventory - inventory is the least liquid and riskiest. It can lose value quickly (obsolescence, going out of season, damage) and isn't guaranteed to sell at the expected price in a short time. The Quick Ratio strips this factor out entirely to answer a stricter question: if the company sold no more goods at all, would it still have enough cash and receivables to pay its short-term debts?
The gap with the Current Ratio is a warning signal

Seasonal fashion chains are the clearest example: most of their current assets sit in seasonal clothing inventory, an asset type that can lose 50-70% of its value if the selling season is missed. When a company's Current Ratio looks high (e.g. 2.5) but its Quick Ratio is low (e.g. 0.8), that's a sign the company's 'liquidity' largely depends on being able to sell its inventory - a far riskier dependency than having cash on hand.

items: The Quick Ratio is most relevant for industries with large, obsolescence-prone inventory: fashion, consumer electronics, technology
Industries with little or no inventory (software, consulting) see almost identical Current and Quick Ratios
A large gap between the two ratios = worth investigating inventory quality and liquidation ability
A Quick Ratio above 1.0 is usually considered safe without needing to depend on selling inventory

lines: When the Current Ratio and Quick Ratio tell two different stories, trust the Quick Ratio more if that industry carries inventory obsolescence risk.
